name: Impact test
seoDesc: Impact test: work out angle of rise (α) from the mass of anvil and the initial elevation of the striker. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the mass of anvil, the initial elevation of the striker, the height of rise and the energy loss and the Impact test calculator solves for angle of rise (α). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Impact test calculator work?
sections.html:
The Impact test calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports angle of rise (α) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the planet); then you type in the mass of anvil (m), the initial elevation of the striker (h), the height of rise (h₁) and the energy loss (Eₗ).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Impact test calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Angle of rise (α)=((energy absorbed (E) + energy loss (Eₗ) + acceleration due to gravity (g) × mass of anvil (m) × center of rotation to striker distance (S) × the cosine of (angle of fall (β))) ÷ (acceleration due to gravity (g) × mass of anvil (m) × center of rotation to striker distance (S)))
Angle of fall (β)=((-initial elevation of the striker (h) + center of rotation to striker distance (S)) ÷ center of rotation to striker distance (S))
Angle of rise (α)=((-height of rise (h₁) + center of rotation to striker distance (S)) ÷ center of rotation to striker distance (S))
Acceleration due to gravity (g)=(1 ÷ 2) × (impact velocity (V) ^ 2) ÷ initial elevation of the striker (h)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Planet set to Earth and Energy loss (Eₗ) = 0 J. Straight away the calculator returns Acceleration due to gravity (g) = 9.8067 m/s².

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Acceleration due to gravity (g) = 9.8067 m/s² should be roughly the size you expected from Planet set to Earth and Energy loss (Eₗ) = 0 J.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Impact test calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the mass of anvil, the initial elevation of the striker and the height of rise — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Impact test calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns angle of rise (α), derived from the mass of anvil, the initial elevation of the striker and the height of rise. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Impact test calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the mass of anvil, the initial elevation of the striker, the height of rise and the energy loss, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter angle of fall (β) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Angle of fall (β) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Acceleration due to gravity (g) = 9.8067 m/s². Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Impact test calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
